forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Salford repays £21m LOBO loan after lender proposes 7.76% rate; £48m more expected to be called
news_drafts.lead:
Salford City Council has repaid a £21m LOBO loan without penalty after the lender exercised its option to propose a new rate of 7.76%, against the 4.75% the loan carried. A LOBO is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The loan had a final maturity of 1 September 2066, according to the council's treasury management mid-year update for 2026/27. The report does not name the lender.

The council took £30m of new long-term borrowing to refinance the loan, and the report says the £21m was repaid from cash balances. Its table of new loans shows two loans from other local authorities, of £15.0m each at 4.90%, maturing in 2029. The council's LOBO balance fell from £163m at 1 April 2026 to £142m at 30 September 2026.

The council has £62m of LOBO loans with call dates before the end of 2026/27. Having taken advice from Arlingclose, it says: "it is considered likely that £48m of these loans will be called." If a higher rate is proposed, the council plans to repay at no additional cost rather than accept revised terms. It would fund any repayment from cash, from other local authorities or from the Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils.

news_drafts.headline: Salford repaid a £21m LOBO loan after lender proposed 7.76%, and expects £48m more to be called
news_drafts.lead:
Salford City Council repaid a £21m LOBO loan in September 2026 after the lender proposed raising its interest rate from 4.75% to 7.76%. A LOBO is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The council's mid-year treasury management report to the Overview and Scrutiny Board says the loan, which had a final maturity of 1 September 2066, was repaid without penalty from cash balances.

The report also records £30m of new three-year borrowing "to refinance" the £21m loan. Its Table 14 lists two £15m loans from other local authorities at 4.90%, maturing in August 2029. The paper does not explain the £9m difference between the £21m repaid and the £30m borrowed.

The council has £62m of LOBO loans with call dates up to 31 March 2027. Following advice from its treasury advisers, Arlingclose, it says: "Based on this assessment, it is considered likely that £48m of these loans will be called." It plans to repay any called loan at no additional cost rather than accept the revised terms. Its LOBO balance fell from £163m on 1 April 2026 to £142m at 30 September 2026.

news_drafts.headline: Salford housing service forecasts £3.6m overspend and cannot meet £1m savings target after mid-year transfer
news_drafts.lead: Salford's housing service, transferred to the Place Directorate mid-year, is forecasting a £3.6m overspend driven by housing benefit subsidy losses and demand pressures in supported housing and housing options. The service cannot deliver its budgeted £1m savings target. In a statement to the scrutiny panel, the council said the service is "not yet sufficiently embedded within the directorate to identify, develop and deliver sustainable savings of this scale without risking service performance" and will need to develop a fresh plan once new leadership arrangements are in place. After drawing £1.76m from reserves, the net overspend stands at £1.8m. The housing capital programme has also been reproffiled down by £17m as contract arrangements are finalised, with the council acknowledging risks to future delivery from staffing and third-party dependencies.

findings.paper_title: 11 Treasury Management Midyear Update Report for 2026-27
findings.headline: The liability benchmark shows additional borrowing will be needed in future years, with the capital financing requirement forecast to rise from £838.6m in 2026/27 to £928.0m in 2028/29.
findings.detail: The paper says the current capital programme and the schemes reprofiled into 2027/28 and 2028/29 mean further borrowing will be required, to be kept under review. Table 24 forecasts the CFR at £895.4m for 2027/28 and £928.0m for 2028/29. Table 11 shows the liability benchmark rising to £426.2m by 2029 against existing borrowing of £285.8m.
findings.matters: A council that moves from holding excess cash to needing new external borrowing will be a larger PWLB and market borrower, which affects its refinancing and funding plans.
findings.figures: £838.6m CFR 2026/27; £895.4m CFR 2027/28; £928.0m CFR 2028/29; £285.8m existing borrowing at 30 September 2026; £426.2m liability benchmark 2029
findings.quote: there would need to be additional borrowing in future years

findings.paper_title: 11 Treasury Management Midyear Update Report for 2026-27
findings.headline: The revised 2026/27 capital programme totals £124.4m, with the borrowing requirement reduced from £75.1m to £56.8m and grants increased from £36.8m to £67.6m.
findings.detail: Table 5 shows the funding mix moving toward grants, reducing the borrowing requirement. Table 4 shows revised capital expenditure of £124.4m against an original estimate of £111.2m. The text of paragraph 5.2 describes the main change as a decrease in forecast spend due to reprofiling, which the table does not show.
findings.matters: A shift from borrowing to grant funding reduces the council's new borrowing need, and the mismatch between the narrative and Table 4 is one a finance reader would want to check against the capital monitoring report.
findings.figures: £124.4m revised capital expenditure; £111.2m original estimate; £75.1m original borrowing requirement; £56.8m revised borrowing requirement; £36.8m original grants; £67.6m revised grants

findings.paper_title: 11 Treasury Management Midyear Update Report for 2026-27
findings.headline: Treasury management costs are reported under budget for the first half of 2026/27, with borrowing interest of £9.78m and investment income of £2.10m each showing zero variance to budget.
findings.detail: The financial implications section says treasury management costs were under budget. Table 18 shows borrowing interest of £9.78m against a mid-year budget of £9.78m and investment income of £2.10m against £2.10m, both with a zero variance. The weighted average investment yield for the first six months was 4.08%, against a Bank Rate of 3.75%, on average balances of about £104m.
findings.matters: A finance officer at another council can compare the 4.08% portfolio yield against the 3.75% Bank Rate to see how the investment book is performing.
findings.figures: £9.78m borrowing interest actual and budget; £2.10m investment income actual and budget; 4.08% weighted average yield; 3.75% Bank Rate; £104m average investments
findings.quote: Treasury management costs were under budget

findings.paper_title: 11 Treasury Management Midyear Update Report for 2026-27
findings.headline: Council proposes funding £5.218m of 2017/18 to 2025/26 Pendleton Tower sprinkler and legal costs from an HRA earmarked reserve, replacing general fund and unsupported borrowing funding.
findings.detail: The review found that the sprinkler works and associated fees relate to HRA assets. The £5.218m comprises sprinkler installation works of £3.624m, capital legal and inspection fees of £0.911m, historic revenue legal fees of £0.598m and current year legal fees of £0.085m. The council proposes to use part of the £14.940m tower block defect compensation received in 2025/26 and held in an HRA earmarked reserve. The paper says this reduces the underlying borrowing need and corrects the historic funding treatment.
findings.matters: A correction moving £5.218m of costs from the general fund and borrowing into the HRA, drawing on defect compensation, is a funding reallocation other councils with housing revenue accounts and similar remediation claims may face.
findings.figures: £5.218m HRA reserve application; £3.624m sprinkler works; £0.911m capital legal and inspection fees; £0.598m historic revenue legal fees; £0.085m current year legal fees; £14.940m compensation held in HRA earmarked reserve
findings.quote: The review has identified historic expenditure of £5.218m incurred between 2017/18 and 2025/26

findings.paper_title: 11 Treasury Management Midyear Update Report for 2026-27
findings.headline: Council expects £48m of its £62m of LOBO loans with call dates before the end of 2026/27 to be called.
findings.detail: The council has £62m of LOBO loans with call dates to the end of the current financial year and has taken advice from Arlingclose on likely exercise. If a higher rate is proposed, the council plans to repay at no additional cost rather than accept revised terms, and would fund any repayment from cash, other local authorities or the PWLB.
findings.matters: Further LOBO repayments would require replacement funding, and the cost of that funding relative to the coupons being retired is a live question for councils with similar LOBO books.
findings.figures: £62m LOBO loans with call dates to year end; £48m likely to be called; £163m LOBO balance at 1 April 2026
findings.quote: Based on this assessment, it is considered likely that £48m of these loans will be called.
